title: Consciousness at the Frontier: Panpsychism and Illusionism
subtitle: Is consciousness everywhere, or nowhere at all?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why the hard problem pushes some philosophers toward radical views, and lay out the options on the table.
By the end you will be able to state the argument for Russellian monism and panpsychism, and explain the combination problem.
By the end you will be able to explain illusionism, the 'illusion problem', and the meta-problem of consciousness.
By the end you will be able to describe integrated information theory, its measure Φ, its surprising predictions and the controversy surrounding it.
hook:
Here are two claims that sound equally absurd. First: the electrons in your coffee cup have some faint glimmer of experience. Second: you have never had a conscious experience in the sense philosophers mean, and the redness of red, as you think of it, does not exist.

On Day 84 you met the **hard problem of consciousness**, David Chalmers's name for the puzzle of why physical processes in the brain are accompanied by subjective experience at all: why there is *something it is like*, in Nagel's phrase, to see red or feel pain. In Lesson 1 you saw that functionalism, despite its successes, struggles with this. Some philosophers have concluded that the hard problem is so hard that only a radical move will solve it. In this final lesson of the Mind track we examine the two most radical options in serious contemporary philosophy, which happen to be opposites: **panpsychism**, which says consciousness is everywhere, and **illusionism**, which says that consciousness, as we usually conceive it, is nowhere. Then we look at a scientific theory that has drawn both admiration and accusations of pseudoscience.

sections.heading: Why the Hard Problem Drives Radical Views
sections.body:
Recall the shape of the problem. Science explains things by describing **structure** and **function**: how parts are arranged and what they do. We can explain how the brain discriminates colors, integrates information and controls speech by describing neural mechanisms. These are what Chalmers called the "easy problems" (easy in principle, not in practice). But after all the functions are explained, a further question seems to remain: why is all this processing accompanied by experience? Why doesn't it go on "in the dark"?

The main options can be laid out as a map.
- **Dualism** (Day 44): consciousness is not physical at all. Chalmers himself defends a form of **property dualism**, holding that experience is a fundamental, non-physical feature of the world, linked to physical processes by psychophysical laws. The cost: it is hard to see how non-physical experiences could cause physical behavior, which threatens to make consciousness causally idle, or **epiphenomenal**.
- **Standard physicalism**: consciousness is a physical process, and the explanatory gap will eventually close, or reflects only a limitation in our concepts. This is the majority view among philosophers, but the hard problem is precisely the doubt that it can work.
- **Panpsychism**: consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of matter. Rather than emerging mysteriously from non-conscious stuff, it was there all along.
- **Illusionism**: phenomenal consciousness, the supposedly ineffable, intrinsic, private qualities of experience, does not exist. What needs explaining is why it *seems* to exist.

Dualism adds something new to the physical world; standard physicalism promises a reduction no one has delivered. Panpsychism and illusionism are both attempts to escape this dilemma, in opposite directions: one by making consciousness more basic, the other by making it less real.

sections.heading: Russellian Monism and Panpsychism
sections.body:
The modern case for panpsychism starts from an observation made by Bertrand Russell in *The Analysis of Matter* (1927), and independently by the physicist Arthur Eddington: physics tells us only about the **structure** and **dispositions** of matter, not about its **intrinsic nature**.

Think about what physics says about mass. Mass is whatever resists acceleration and produces gravitational attraction. Charge is whatever attracts and repels other charges in certain ways. Every physical property is defined by what it does: its relations to other things and its effects on measuring instruments. Physics is, in Russell's view, a description of a vast causal network, specified mathematically. But a network of relations seems to need something that stands in the relations. What are the things in the network intrinsically, in themselves? Physics is silent.

Now consider: there is exactly one place where we seem to know something about the intrinsic nature of matter from the inside, namely our own brains, when we have experiences. Russell suggested that the intrinsic nature of matter, at least in brains, might be experiential. Generalize this and you get **Russellian monism**: the intrinsic natures underlying physical structure are themselves experiential (or **protophenomenal**, the building blocks of experience). Physics describes what matter does; consciousness is what matter is.

This view has striking advantages. It solves the hard problem by placing experience in the foundations, so it does not need to be produced from non-experiential ingredients. And it avoids the dualist's causal problem: experience is not an extra ingredient, but the intrinsic nature of the very things that do the causing in physics, so consciousness is causally efficacious after all.

Galen Strawson's influential paper "Realistic Monism: Why Physicalism Entails Panpsychism" (2006) argued that any physicalist who takes consciousness seriously must accept panpsychism, because experience cannot emerge from wholly non-experiential stuff: such emergence would be a kind of miracle. Philip Goff's *Galileo's Error* (2019) argued that modern science, since Galileo deliberately set aside sensory qualities in order to describe nature mathematically, was designed to leave consciousness out, so it is no surprise that it cannot find it.

Panpsychism does not say that rocks or coffee cups are conscious. It says that the fundamental constituents of matter have extremely simple forms of experience, and that only certain kinds of organization, such as brains, combine these into rich unified minds. A rock is a mere aggregate, without a unified point of view.

sections.heading: The Combination Problem
sections.body:
But that last claim leads to panpsychism's deepest difficulty, known as the **combination problem**: how do the tiny experiences of particles combine to form the unified experience of a human being?

William James stated the problem vividly in *The Principles of Psychology* (1890), long before modern panpsychism. Take a sentence of a dozen words, he wrote, and twelve men, and give each man one word. Then stand the men in a row and let each think of his word as intently as he will; nowhere will there be a consciousness of the whole sentence. Putting experiences side by side does not create a new experience that contains them.

The problem has several aspects.
- **The subject-summing problem.** Each particle, on panpsychism, is a little subject of experience. How can many subjects make up one subject? It seems that subjects are not the kind of thing that can be added together; each has its own point of view.
- **The quality problem.** We experience a vast range of qualities: colors, tastes, emotions. If particles have only a few basic qualities, how do these combine into the experienced redness of a tomato?
- **The structure problem.** The structure of our experience (a visual field, a stream of thoughts) does not seem to match the structure of the brain's physical activity in any obvious way.

Panpsychists have offered responses. Goff has proposed a **phenomenal bonding** relation, which, when it holds among subjects, makes them constitute a larger subject; we do not know its nature, but physics may describe it from the outside. Some prefer **panprotopsychism**, where the fundamental properties are not themselves experiences but proto-experiential properties that collectively constitute experience; this avoids subject-summing but risks reintroducing a hard problem of how protophenomenal properties yield phenomenal ones. Others, such as Goff and Itay Shani, defend **cosmopsychism**: the universe as a whole is the fundamental conscious subject, and individual minds are aspects of it. This trades the combination problem for a **decomposition problem**: how does one cosmic mind divide into many?

None of these responses is yet widely accepted, and the combination problem remains for panpsychism what the hard problem is for physicalism: the place where the view must do its hardest work.

sections.heading: Illusionism: Consciousness as a Trick of Introspection
sections.body:
Illusionism takes the opposite path. Its leading defenders are Daniel Dennett, in works such as "Quining Qualia" (1988) and *Consciousness Explained* (1991), and Keith Frankish, whose paper "Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness" (2016) gave the view its name and its modern form.

Illusionists make a careful distinction. They do not deny that we see, hear, feel pain or are awake. They deny the existence of **phenomenal consciousness** in the philosopher's sense: intrinsic, ineffable, private, directly known qualities of experience, the qualia of Lesson 1. These, they argue, are an introspective illusion. When we introspect, our brains represent our own perceptual states as having these special qualities, much as a magic trick leads us to represent a coin as having vanished. The representation is real; the special qualities it attributes are not.

Why believe this? Illusionists offer several arguments.
- **Theoretical economy.** If the special qualities of experience existed, they would have to be non-physical or physically mysterious. Better to deny them than to rewrite physics.
- **The meta-problem.** Chalmers himself (2018) pointed out that there is a further, "easy" problem: explaining why we *say* and *think* there is a hard problem. This is a question about behavior and cognition, so it should have a functional explanation. Once we have that explanation, illusionists say, there is nothing left to explain. Chalmers agrees the meta-problem is important, though he denies that solving it would dissolve the hard problem.
- **Unreliability of introspection.** Psychology has shown that introspection is error-prone. We misjudge how detailed our visual field is (we notice remarkably little outside the center of attention, as experiments on change blindness and inattentional blindness show), and we misreport the causes of our behavior. Why trust it about the metaphysics of experience?

The main objection seems overwhelming at first: an illusion is a kind of experience. If it seems to me that I am in pain, isn't that seeming itself an experience? Galen Strawson has called the denial of consciousness the silliest claim ever made. Illusionists reply that the "seeming" in question is a representational state, a kind of judgment or registration in the brain, which need not have phenomenal properties itself. The illusion is not experienced, in the special sense; it is represented. Whether this reply succeeds, or quietly changes the subject, is the central question in this debate.

The disagreement has an unusual structure. Panpsychists and illusionists agree that standard physicalism cannot simply explain phenomenal consciousness. They disagree about whether to conclude that consciousness is more fundamental than we thought, or less real.

sections.heading: Integrated Information Theory and the Science of Consciousness
sections.body:
Alongside these philosophical views, neuroscientists have developed scientific theories of consciousness. The most philosophically ambitious is **integrated information theory** (IIT), developed by the neuroscientist Giulio Tononi from 2004 onward and championed by Christof Koch.

IIT starts not from the brain but from experience itself. It identifies what it takes to be essential properties of every experience: it exists intrinsically, for itself; it is structured; it is specific (this experience, not another); it is unified (you cannot experience the left half of your visual field independently of the right); and it is definite. It then asks what physical properties a system must have to account for these. Its answer is **integrated information**, measured by a quantity called **Φ** (phi): roughly, how much a system's causal structure as a whole constrains its own past and future states beyond what its parts do independently. A system is conscious, according to IIT, to the degree that it has high Φ, and the content of its experience corresponds to the shape of its causal structure.

IIT makes some testable and some startling predictions.
- The **cerebellum** contains most of the brain's neurons, yet damage to it rarely affects consciousness. IIT explains this: the cerebellum's parallel, modular organization yields low integration.
- A conventional digital computer, even one simulating a human brain perfectly, would have very low Φ because of the way its hardware is wired. So IIT denies that functional duplication is sufficient for consciousness, directly contradicting the functionalism of Lesson 1 and Chalmers's organizational invariance.
- Simple systems with the right architecture, such as a large grid of logic gates, could have very high Φ, and so, according to the computer scientist Scott Aaronson's critique (2014), be more conscious than humans while doing nothing intelligent. Tononi accepted the implication.

IIT thus has panpsychist features: consciousness is graded and present wherever integration exists, though it is not present in mere aggregates.

IIT has become one of the most controversial theories in science. In 2023 a large "adversarial collaboration," in which proponents of IIT and its rival, **global workspace theory** (which links consciousness to the broadcasting of information across the brain), agreed in advance on experiments that could favor one or the other, reported results that challenged key predictions of both theories. Later that year, more than a hundred researchers signed an open letter calling IIT pseudoscience, chiefly because of its untestable panpsychist implications; many other scientists criticized the letter as an unhelpful way to conduct a scientific dispute. The same year, Koch formally lost a 25-year bet with Chalmers, made in 1998, that a clear neural signature of consciousness would be found by 2023, and paid it with a case of fine wine.

The frontier, then, is genuinely open. As in so many lessons of this course, the deepest questions turn out to be the oldest ones, now asked with new tools.

keyQuote.text: Physics is mathematical not because we know so much about the physical world, but because we know so little: it is only its mathematical properties that we can discover.
keyQuote.source: Bertrand Russell, An Outline of Philosophy (1927)

modernConnection.title: Could an AI Be Conscious? It Depends on Which Theory Is True
modernConnection.body:
In 2022 a Google engineer, Blake Lemoine, claimed that the company's chatbot LaMDA was sentient; Google rejected the claim and later dismissed him. Most experts agreed with Google, but the episode made a once-academic question urgent. In 2023 a group of nineteen researchers, led by Patrick Butlin and Robert Long and including both philosophers and neuroscientists, published a report on consciousness in artificial intelligence. Their method was to take leading scientific theories, such as global workspace theory and higher-order theories, and derive "indicator properties" that a conscious system should have. They concluded that no current AI system was a strong candidate for consciousness, but that there were no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy many of the indicators.

The theories in this lesson give radically different verdicts.
- On **functionalism** with organizational invariance, an AI with the right functional organization would be conscious, whatever it is made of.
- On **IIT**, a conventional digital computer would have negligible consciousness however intelligently it behaved, while unusual hardware might be conscious.
- On **panpsychism**, the fundamental constituents of a computer have some form of experience, but whether the whole system is a unified subject depends on how the combination problem is solved.
- On **illusionism**, the question becomes whether the AI represents itself as having experiences in the way we represent ourselves. If that is all our consciousness is, an AI with a similar self-model would have just as much claim to it.

The practical stakes are large. If AI systems could suffer, creating them in huge numbers would raise moral questions like those of population ethics (Ethics track, Lesson 5). A similar logic has extended concern to animals: in April 2024, a group of scientists and philosophers signed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness, stating that there is strong scientific support for consciousness in mammals and birds and at least a realistic possibility of it in many other animals, including fish, octopuses and insects. Whatever the right theory, we are increasingly forced to decide how to act under uncertainty about which beings have an inner life.

vocabulary.definition: The view that consciousness, or something like it, is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world.
vocabulary.example: A panpsychist holds that electrons have extremely simple experiences, which combine in brains to form rich minds.

vocabulary.definition: The view that physics describes only the structure and dispositions of matter, and that its intrinsic nature is experiential or proto-experiential.
vocabulary.example: According to Russellian monism, what mass is in itself may be something akin to experience.

vocabulary.definition: The problem, for panpsychism, of explaining how tiny micro-experiences combine to form unified macro-experiences like ours.
vocabulary.example: William James's twelve men, each thinking one word, illustrate the combination problem.

vocabulary.definition: The view that phenomenal consciousness, in the sense of intrinsic, ineffable qualities of experience, does not exist, but introspection represents us as having it.
vocabulary.example: An illusionist says the redness you seem to experience is a representation, not a special inner quality.

vocabulary.definition: Chalmers's name for the problem of explaining why we think and say there is a hard problem of consciousness.
vocabulary.example: Solving the meta-problem would explain why philosophers write books about qualia.

vocabulary.definition: The view that conscious experiences are caused by physical processes but have no causal effects themselves.
vocabulary.example: Epiphenomenalism implies that your pain plays no role in making you pull your hand away from the stove.

vocabulary.definition: Tononi's theory that consciousness corresponds to integrated information (Φ), the degree to which a system's causal structure as a whole exceeds that of its parts.
vocabulary.example: Integrated information theory explains why the cerebellum, despite its many neurons, contributes little to consciousness.

vocabulary.definition: The view that the universe as a whole is the fundamental conscious subject, with individual minds as derivative aspects of it.
vocabulary.example: Cosmopsychism replaces the combination problem with the problem of how one cosmic mind divides into many.

thinkingExercise.title: Choose Your Mystery
thinkingExercise.prompt: Every theory of consciousness accepts something strange. Decide which strangeness you can live with.
steps: Write one sentence stating, as precisely as you can, what you mean by your own consciousness right now.
Read your sentence as an illusionist would. Which part of it, if any, could be a misrepresentation by your brain? Which part seems impossible to doubt?
Imagine explaining panpsychism to a skeptical friend. Give the strongest argument for it (Russell's structure argument) and the strongest objection (the combination problem).
Rank dualism, physicalism, panpsychism and illusionism from most to least plausible, giving the main cost you see in each.
Decide what your top-ranked view implies for whether a future AI could be conscious, and whether that would change how you think it should be treated.

summary: The hard problem pushes some philosophers beyond dualism and standard physicalism toward two opposite radical views: panpsychism and illusionism.

Russellian monism holds that physics describes only structure and dispositions, leaving the intrinsic nature of matter, which may be experiential; this underlies modern panpsychism (Strawson, Goff) and gives consciousness a causal role.
The combination problem, anticipated by William James, asks how micro-experiences make up unified minds; responses include phenomenal bonding, panprotopsychism and cosmopsychism.

Illusionism (Dennett, Frankish) denies phenomenal consciousness and seeks to explain why it seems to exist, linking to Chalmers's meta-problem; critics say an illusion of experience is itself an experience.
Integrated information theory identifies consciousness with integrated information (Φ), making striking predictions about the cerebellum, computers and simple grids, and remains highly controversial.

quiz.question: What is the key observation behind Russellian monism?
options: Physics describes the structure and dispositions of matter but not its intrinsic nature
quiz.explanation: Russell and Eddington noted that physics defines its properties by what they do, leaving open what matter is in itself.

quiz.question: Panpsychism holds that rocks and coffee cups have unified conscious experiences.
quiz.explanation: Panpsychism attributes simple experience to fundamental constituents; mere aggregates like rocks lack a unified point of view.

quiz.question: William James's example of twelve men, each thinking one word of a sentence, illustrates:
quiz.explanation: Putting experiences side by side does not produce a new experience that contains them all.

quiz.question: Which view swaps the combination problem for a 'decomposition problem'?
quiz.explanation: If the universe is the fundamental subject, we must explain how it divides into many individual minds.

quiz.question: What does illusionism deny?
options: That there are intrinsic, ineffable, phenomenal qualities of experience
quiz.explanation: Illusionists accept perception and wakefulness but deny phenomenal consciousness in the philosopher's special sense.

quiz.question: The meta-problem of consciousness is the problem of explaining why we think and say that there is a hard problem.
quiz.explanation: Chalmers introduced the term; illusionists think solving it would leave nothing more to explain, while Chalmers disagrees.

quiz.question: According to integrated information theory, why does the cerebellum contribute little to consciousness despite its many neurons?
options: Its modular, parallel organization produces low integrated information
It is not made of neurons
It is not connected to the rest of the brain
quiz.explanation: IIT ties consciousness to integration, not to the number of neurons.

quiz.question: IIT implies that a digital computer perfectly simulating a human brain would be just as conscious as the brain.
quiz.explanation: IIT holds that conventional computer hardware has low Φ however it behaves, so it denies that functional duplication is sufficient for consciousness.

quiz.question: A researcher argues that an AI that represents itself as having experiences, in the same way we do, has as much claim to consciousness as we do. Which view does this most closely reflect?
quiz.explanation: If our consciousness consists in our self-representations, a system with similar self-representations would have the same kind of consciousness.

goDeeper.body:
A deep question underlying this lesson is whether consciousness is the kind of thing that admits of **vagueness**. In the Logic track you met the Sorites paradox: "heap" and "bald" have borderline cases. Many physical and biological categories are similar: there is no sharp line between a living and a non-living virus-like particle. But consider consciousness. Michael Tye and others have argued that consciousness seems to be **all-or-nothing**: it seems that either there is something it is like to be a system or there is not, with no borderline cases, since a "borderline experience" would still be an experience. If that is right, then on a gradual evolutionary or developmental story, there must have been a sharp moment at which consciousness first appeared, which seems arbitrary. Panpsychists use this as an argument: the only non-arbitrary place for a sharp line is at the very bottom, so consciousness must be present all the way down. Illusionists reply that this is another symptom of the illusion: real processes are graded, and the sense that consciousness must be all-or-nothing reflects how introspection represents it.

A second advanced topic is **higher-order theories** of consciousness, which offer a middle way between these extremes. On David Rosenthal's higher-order thought theory, a mental state is conscious when one has a suitable thought about being in it. This explains consciousness in functional terms without denying it outright, and it figures among the theories used to assess AI. Critics ask whether a thought about a state could make that state feel like something, or merely make it accessible.

Finally, some philosophers, notably Colin McGinn, defend **mysterianism**: the solution to the hard problem exists, but human minds, with their particular cognitive structure, may be incapable of grasping it, as a dog cannot grasp calculus. This is a sobering thought on which to end a course: some questions may outlast every lesson.

readings.note: A lively, accessible case for panpsychism, written for a general audience.

readings.author: Keith Frankish (editor)

readings.author: Daniel Dennett
readings.note: The classic sustained argument against the Cartesian theater and qualia.

readings.author: Christof Koch

questions: Which is harder to believe: that electrons have experiences, or that you do not have phenomenal consciousness?
If a theory of consciousness cannot be tested, is it still science? Is it still worth believing?
How should we treat beings, animal or artificial, when we are genuinely uncertain whether they are conscious?
